items.readable_text:
Content:
A local extremum (or relative extremum) of a function is a point that is either a maximum or minimum point of the function relative to an (open) interval in the function's domain.

Content:
For example, consider the function shown in the graph below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/cc94a2c8ca5bf492c7746b6f57716f90]

Content:
The graph has a peak at the point [MATH: A] where [MATH: x=0.] We say that the function has a local maximum when [MATH: x=0.] We also say that the point [MATH: A] is a local maximum point of the function.

Content:
This means that we can take an open interval of [MATH: x]-values around [MATH: x=0] such that [MATH: A] will be the highest point on the graph in this interval.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/cd135a08e4ea075aa612fe6fa3143875]

Content:
Similarly, the graph has a valley at the point [MATH: B] where [MATH: x=2.] We say that the function has a local minimum when [MATH: x=2.] We can also say that the point [MATH: B] is a local minimum point of the function.

Content:
This means that we can take an open interval of [MATH: x]-values around [MATH: x=2] such that [MATH: B] will be the lowest point on the graph in this interval.

The point [MATH: A] where [MATH: x=0] is a local maximum of [MATH: f(x)] because we can draw an open interval around [MATH: x=0] such that the point [MATH: A] is the highest point on the graph. One such interval is [MATH: x\in (-0.5,0.5),] shown below:

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's examine each of the given points in turn.

  • The function has a local minimum at [MATH: x=0.] For example, in the interval [MATH: (-0.5,0.5),] the smallest value of the function is attained at [MATH: x=0,] as shown below.

    We can write this mathematically as [MATH: f(x) \ge f(0) \:] for all [MATH: \: x \in (-0.5,0.5).]

  • The function does not have a local minimum at [MATH: x=1.] For any open interval containing [MATH: x=1], there will be points on the graph that lie below [MATH: f(1)].

  • The function has a local minimum at [MATH: x=3.] For example, in the interval [MATH: (2.5,3.5),] the smallest value of the function is attained at [MATH: x=3,] as shown below.

    We can write this mathematically as [MATH: f(x) \ge f(3) \:] for all [MATH: \: x \in (2.5,3.5).]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: f(x)] be the function shown below. Which of the following statements are true?

  1. [MATH: f(x)] attains a local maximum at [MATH: x=-2]

  2. [MATH: f(x)] attains a local minimum at [MATH: x=2]

  3. [MATH: f(x)] attains a local maximum at [MATH: x=0]

Let [MATH: f(x)] be the function shown below. Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: f(x)] attains a local maximum at [MATH: x=-2]
2. [MATH: f(x)] attains a local minimum at [MATH: x=2]
3. [MATH: f(x)] attains a local maximum at [MATH: x=0]

[IMG: /graphics/72a605f5ef639ece2269919e92397db4]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's examine each of the given statements in turn.

  • Statement I is false. The function has a local minimum at [MATH: x=-2.] For example, in the interval [MATH: (-2.5,-1.5),] the smallest value of the function is attained at [MATH: x=-2,] as shown below.

    We can write this mathematically as [MATH: f(x) \ge f(-2) \:] for all [MATH: \: x \in (-2.5,-1.5).]

  • Statement II is true. The function has a local minimum at [MATH: x=2.] For example, in the interval [MATH: (1.5,2.5),] the smallest value of the function is attained at [MATH: x=2,] as shown below.

    We can write this mathematically as [MATH: f(x) \ge f(2) \:] for all [MATH: \: x \in (1.5,2.5).]

  • Statement III is true. The function has a local maximum at [MATH: x=0.] For example, in the interval [MATH: (-0.5,0.5),] the greatest value of the function is attained at [MATH: x=0,] as shown below.

    We can write this mathematically as [MATH: f(x) \le f(0) \:] for all [MATH: \: x \in (-0.5,0.5).]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A local extremum (or relative extremum) of a function is a point that is either a maximum or minimum point of the function relative to an (open) interval in the function's domain.

Content:
For example, consider the function shown in the graph below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/cc94a2c8ca5bf492c7746b6f57716f90]

Content:
The graph has a peak at the point [MATH: A] where [MATH: x=0.] We say that the function has a local maximum when [MATH: x=0.] We also say that the point [MATH: A] is a local maximum point of the function.

Content:
This means that we can take an open interval of [MATH: x]-values around [MATH: x=0] such that [MATH: A] will be the highest point on the graph in this interval.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/cd135a08e4ea075aa612fe6fa3143875]

Content:
Similarly, the graph has a valley at the point [MATH: B] where [MATH: x=2.] We say that the function has a local minimum when [MATH: x=2.] We can also say that the point [MATH: B] is a local minimum point of the function.

Content:
This means that we can take an open interval of [MATH: x]-values around [MATH: x=2] such that [MATH: B] will be the lowest point on the graph in this interval.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3fa7269d76f62e8205d22a80b040f664]

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying the Local Extrema of a Function Visually

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Consider the point [MATH: U.] We can take an open interval of [MATH: x]-values such that [MATH: U] will be the highest point on the graph in this interval. So, [MATH: U] is a local maximum.

A similar interval exists for the point [MATH: W,] too. So, [MATH: W] is also a local maximum.

[IMG: /graphics/0f3c2aedcbb9d00fc33368d244640933]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Writing a Condition for a Point To Be a Local Extremum

The point [MATH: A] where [MATH: x=0] is a local maximum of [MATH: f(x)] because we can draw an open interval around [MATH: x=0] such that the point [MATH: A] is the highest point on the graph. One such interval is [MATH: x\in (-0.5,0.5),] shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a9d40bac5a915b1de2b353418291842a]

Content:
Everywhere in this interval, the value of the function is less than or equal to [MATH: f(0),] the largest value of the function in this interval. We can write this mathematically as

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: f(x) \leq f(0)] for all [MATH: x\in(-0.5, 0.5).]

Content:
Similarly, the point [MATH: B] where [MATH: x=2] is a local minimum of [MATH: f(x)] because we can draw an open interval around [MATH: x=2] such that the point [MATH: B] is the lowest point on the graph. One such interval is [MATH: x\in (1.5,2.5),] shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b6e77049745968a191831ba7067d343f]

Content:
Everywhere in this interval, the value of the function is greater than or equal to [MATH: f(2),] the smallest value of the function in this interval. We can write this mathematically as

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: f(x) \geq f(2)] for all [MATH: x\in(1.5, 2.5).]
